data.comment: heading of the /about section crediting standing sources

data.name: about.reading.standing.lead

data.comment: lead half of a point; the .body half completes the same sentence

data.name: about.reading.standing.body
data.value: Both are read on a schedule, with permission, and both are credited below. Every other address here is one this crawler found by probing.

data.name: about.reading.labelled.lead
data.value: What they tell us is labelled as theirs.

data.name: about.reading.labelled.body
data.value: A name or a genre one of them holds is shown as something that source says, never as something we measured — and where our own probe disagrees, the disagreement is what you see.

data.name: about.feed.aresCentral.note
data.value: The AresMUSH community's own hub. Its maintainer issued us API credentials, and we read its games list hourly: the addresses, and what each game says about itself there.
data.comment: what one standing source gives us; AresMUSH and AresCentral are proper nouns

data.name: about.feed.intermud3.note
data.value: A network many LP-family games are joined to. We take its list of addresses, and ask the games that answer how many people are connected.
data.comment: what one standing source gives us

data.name: about.lede
data.value: Every game here was measured by the crawler, and every value says where it came from and when. This page covers what we gather, its limits, what we won't do, and how to make the crawler stop.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.heading
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.declared.lead
data.value: Measured beats declared, and both are shown.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.declared.body
data.value: A game's MSSP report is the game describing itself. The telnet handshake is what we watched it do. Both appear on its page, labelled with how and when. Where they disagree, we show the disagreement.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.count.lead
data.value: A player count says where it came from.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.count.body
data.value: Either a WHO or DOING read at the connect screen, which we counted, or the game's own MSSP PLAYERS field, which it published. Never merged.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.unknown.lead
data.value: Only a completed read can be a zero. Anything else is unknown.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.unknown.body
data.value: Servers customise their WHO headers freely, and past a point our parser cannot read one. That is uncountable, its own state. A measured zero — we got in, nobody was there — is a count, and prints as one.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.reachable.lead
data.value: We call this reachable. We never call it uptime.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.reachable.body
data.value: We open a socket from one host at intervals. A game we cannot route to is unreachable and perfectly alive. Nothing here claims a game's uptime, because nothing here measured it.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.hour.lead
data.value: An hour is counted, uncountable, or not measured.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.measures.hour.body
data.value: The activity grid has three states. The third is empty and names no cause: an hour we could not reach and an hour we never probed are the same absence, and neither is that server's downtime.
data.comment: about: the page, and what a fact here is

data.name: about.limits.heading
data.value: How we gather and adjust data
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.grace.lead
data.value: Archive grace is measured from the day we found you.
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.grace.body
data.value: A game that stops answering leaves the default listing after its grace period: a quarter of the reachable time we probed, floored at 60 days and capped at 365. A game running since 1995 starts at the floor on the day we discover it. We import nothing to fill in the years before we arrived.
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.created.lead
data.value: We do not credit MSSP CREATED toward that grace.
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.created.body
data.value: It is one hand-typed line in a config file, so crediting it would make the archive threshold gameable. We also can't guess at its format.
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.claim.lead
data.value: Claiming a game earns the ceiling.
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.claim.body

data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.deletion.lead
data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.limits.deletion.body

data.comment: about: what we know we get wrong

data.name: about.crawler.heading
data.value: The crawler, and how to make it stop
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.probe.lead
data.value: A probe is one connection that never logs in.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.probe.body
data.value: It opens a socket, negotiates telnet options, reads the connect screen, asks for MSSP by negotiating option 70, sends {commands}, and disconnects. No character, no login, nothing changed on the far side. A timeout bounds the session so a wedged probe cannot sit on a connection slot.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.delay.lead
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.delay.body
data.value: A game that states a preferred minimum gap in its MSSP report is heeded. A dark game is still tried for ever at the longer interval, which is how it re-lists itself when it comes back.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.referral.lead
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.referral.body
data.value: MSSP lets a game name other games. We use the endpoint as the source of truth however.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.screens.lead
data.value: Connect screens are shown because they are sent to everybody.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.screens.body
data.value: Claiming a game gives its owner the option to stop it being shown.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.stop.lead
data.value: Say stop, and we stop — three ways.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.stop.body
data.value: Publish {variable} 1 in your MSSP report, and the probe that reads it is the last one. Or publish a TXT record at {label}.your.host reading "{value}", which needs no MSSP support and no account here. Or write to a person. All three are honoured within one crawl cycle, recorded with the date and what we read, and enforced on the submission form too.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.scope.lead
data.value: The MSSP field stops that listener; the record stops the host.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.scope.body
data.value: MSSP is published by the port that answered, so it speaks for that port — MU* hosting routinely runs unrelated games on one domain, and one must not silence its neighbour. A TXT record covers every port unless it names one, as "{value}=4201". Anything there we cannot read as a port list means the whole host, so "{value}=all" works.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.dns.lead
data.value: The DNS route is the one you can undo without asking us.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.dns.body
data.value: A TXT record is readable without connecting to a server that told us not to, so we re-read it before every dial. Delete it and we dial again within a week. An MSSP field cannot be re-read without doing the thing you asked us to stop, so MSSP opt-outs and written requests stand until you say otherwise. That TXT lookup is all an opted-out address gets: it touches your nameserver, never your game.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.stopping.lead
data.value: Stopping is not deleting, and it is not downtime.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.stopping.body
data.value: A game that opts out keeps its page, its address and everything we measured before it asked. Only new data stops: the activity grid stops gaining hours and names no cause, because our decision to stop knocking is a fact about us. It is recorded on the crawl that did not happen, and in the register of who asked.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.unlist.lead
data.value: If stopping is not enough, the listing can go too.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop

data.name: about.crawler.unlist.body
data.value: Once we have stopped on every address your game answers on, your dashboard offers one more thing: take it out of the listing, the rankings and the daily figure. The page and every address it has ever had still answer, and nothing is deleted — it stops being somewhere a reader arrives by browsing. It needs a verified claim, because it is a decision about your game and we record who made it. And a probe undoes it: take your opt-out back, and the next dial that gets an answer puts you back in the listing without asking us twice.
data.comment: about: the crawler, and how to make it stop
